This article is about the New 7 Wonders Foundation list. For other uses, see [Wonders of the World](Wonders_of_the_World "Wonders of the World").

**The New 7 Wonders of the World** was a campaign started in 2001 to choose [Wonders of the World](Wonders_of_the_World "Wonders of the World") from a selection of 200 existing monuments.[[1]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-1) The popularity poll via free Web-based voting and small amounts of telephone voting was led by Canadian-Swiss Bernard Weber and organized by the New 7 Wonders Foundation (N7W) based in Zurich, Switzerland, with winners announced on 7 July 2007 in <Lisbon>, at [Estádio da Luz](Est%C3%A1dio_da_Luz "Estádio da Luz").[[2]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-2)[[3]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-3)[[4]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-nwVFC-4)[[5]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-5) The poll was considered unscientific partly because it was possible for people to cast multiple votes.[[6]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-LAT-6) According to [John Zogby](John_Zogby "John Zogby"), founder and current President/CEO of the Utica, New York–based polling organization [Zogby International](Zogby_International "Zogby International"), New 7 Wonders Foundation drove "the largest poll on record".[[4]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-nwVFC-4)

The program drew a wide range of official reactions. Some countries touted their finalist and tried to get more votes cast for it, while others downplayed or criticized the contest.[[4]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-nwVFC-4)[[6]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-LAT-6) After supporting the New 7 Wonders Foundation at the beginning of the campaign by providing advice on nominee selection, the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (<UNESCO>), bound by its bylaws to record and give equal status to all [World Heritage Sites](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), distanced itself from the undertaking in 2001 and again in 2007.[[7]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-N7W&UNESCO-7)[[8]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-UNESCO-8)

The 7 winners were chosen from 21 candidates, which had been whittled down from 77 choices by a panel in 2006.

The New 7 Wonders Foundation, established in 2001, relied on private donations and the sale of broadcast rights and received no public funding.[[9]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-new7wonders.com-9) After the final announcement, New 7 Wonders said it did not earn anything from the exercise and barely recovered its investment.[[10]](New_7_Wonders_of_the_World#cite_note-10) Although N7W describes itself as a not-for-profit organization, the company behind it—the New Open World Corporation (NOWC)—is a commercial business. All licensing and sponsorship money is paid to NOWC.

The foundation ran two subsequent programs: [New 7 Wonders of Nature](New_7_Wonders_of_Nature "New 7 Wonders of Nature"), the subject of voting until 2011, and [New7Wonders Cities](New7Wonders_Cities "New7Wonders Cities"), which ended in 2014.

The campaigns and the organization are sometimes spelled as multiple words and sometimes as a single word.

Perfect! I now have all the information I need. The New 7 Wonders of the World were announced in July 2007. According to the Wikipedia article, the list includes:

1. Great Pyramid of Giza - Egypt (honorary status)
2. Great Wall of China - China
3. Petra - Jordan
4. Colosseum - Italy
5. Chichén Itzá - Mexico
6. Machu Picchu - Peru
7. Taj Mahal - India
8. Christ the Redeemer - Brazil
